title: Book 3 — Telemachus visits Nestor at Pylos
paragraphs: As the sun rose from the beautiful sea into the heavens to bring light to mortals and immortals alike, they reached Pylos, the city of Neleus. The people of Pylos had gathered on the seashore to sacrifice black bulls to Poseidon, lord of earthquakes. There were nine groups of five hundred men each, with nine bulls for each group. As they ate the sacred meats and burned the thigh bones on the coals in Poseidon's honor, Telemachus and his crew arrived, furled their sails, anchored their ship, and came ashore.

Athena led the way with Telemachus following her. Soon she said, "Telemachus, you mustn't be shy or nervous at all. You've taken this voyage to try to find out where your father is buried and how he died, so go straight up to Nestor and see what he can tell us. Ask him to speak the truth, and he won't lie to you—he's an excellent man."

"But how, Mentor," Telemachus replied, "can I approach Nestor, and how should I address him? I've never been used to having long conversations with people, and I'm embarrassed to start questioning someone so much older than myself."
"Some things, Telemachus," Athena answered, "will come to you by instinct, and the gods will inspire you further. I'm certain that the gods have been with you from birth until now."

She then walked quickly ahead, and Telemachus followed her steps until they reached the place where the groups of Pylian people were assembled. There they found Nestor sitting with his sons, while his companions busily prepared dinner, putting pieces of meat on spits while other pieces cooked. When they saw the strangers, they crowded around them, took them by the hand, and invited them to sit down. Nestor's son Pisistratus immediately offered his hand to each of them and seated them on soft sheepskins that lay on the sand near his father and his brother Thrasymedes. Then he gave them portions of the sacred meat and poured wine into a golden cup, handing it first to Athena and greeting her respectfully.

"Offer a prayer, sir," he said, "to Lord Poseidon, for you're joining his feast. When you've properly prayed and made your drink offering, pass the cup to your friend so he can do the same. I'm sure he too lifts his hands in prayer, for no one can live without God in this world. Still, he's younger than you and about my own age, so I'll give you precedence."

As he spoke, he handed her the cup. Athena thought it very proper of him to have given it to her first. She began praying earnestly to Poseidon: "O you who encircle the earth, grant the prayers of your servants who call upon you. Especially we pray that you send down your grace on Nestor and his sons. Also give the rest of the Pylian people some worthy return for the fine sacrifice they're offering you. Finally, grant Telemachus and me success in the matter that brought us in our ship to Pylos."

When she finished praying, she handed the cup to Telemachus, and he prayed as well. Soon, when the outer meats were roasted and taken off the spits, the carvers gave everyone their portion and they all had an excellent dinner. As soon as they'd eaten and drunk enough, Nestor, the knight of Gerenia, began to speak.

"Now," he said, "that our guests have finished their dinner, it's time to ask who they are. Who are you, strangers, and from what port have you sailed? Are you traders, or do you sail the seas as pirates with your hand against every man, and every man's hand against you?"
Telemachus answered boldly, for Athena had given him courage to ask about his father and make a good name for himself.

"Nestor," he said, "son of Neleus, honor of the Greek people, you ask where we come from, and I'll tell you. We come from Ithaca below Mount Neriton, and what I want to discuss is a private matter, not public. I seek news of my unfortunate father Odysseus, who's said to have destroyed Troy alongside you. We know what fate befell each of the other heroes who fought at Troy, but regarding Odysseus, heaven has hidden from us even the knowledge that he's dead, for no one can tell us where he died, or whether he fell in battle on the mainland or was lost at sea in the waves. Therefore I come as a suppliant to you, hoping you might tell me of his sad end—whether you saw it with your own eyes or heard it from some other traveler, for he was born to suffer. Don't soften the truth out of pity for me, but tell me plainly exactly what you saw. If my brave father Odysseus ever served you loyally, either in word or deed, when you Greeks were hard-pressed among the Trojans, remember it now in my favor and tell me the truth."

"My friend," Nestor answered, "you bring back memories of great sorrow, for the brave Greeks suffered much both at sea while raiding under Achilles, and fighting before the great city of King Priam. All our best men fell there—Ajax, Achilles, Patroclus who was like a god in counsel, and my own dear son Antilochus, remarkably swift of foot and brave in battle. But we suffered much more than this. What mortal tongue could tell the whole story? Even if you stayed here questioning me for five or six years, I couldn't tell you all that the Greeks endured, and you'd turn homeward weary of my tale before it ended. For nine long years we tried every kind of strategy, but heaven's hand was against us. During all this time, no one could match your father in cleverness—if you are indeed his son—I can hardly believe my eyes—and you speak just like him too. No one would think people of such different ages could speak so similarly. He and I never disagreed from first to last, neither in camp nor council, but with one heart and purpose we advised the Greeks how everything might turn out for the best.

"However, when we had sacked Priam's city and were setting sail as heaven had scattered us, Zeus decided to torment the Greeks on their homeward voyage. They hadn't all been wise or understanding, so many came to a bad end through the anger of Zeus's daughter Athena, who caused a quarrel between the two sons of Atreus.

"The sons of Atreus called a meeting that wasn't properly done, for it was sunset and the Greeks were heavy with wine. When they explained why they'd gathered the people, it seemed Menelaus wanted to sail home immediately, which displeased Agamemnon, who thought we should wait until we'd offered sacrifices to appease Athena's anger. Fool that he was, he should have known he wouldn't prevail with her, for when the gods make up their minds, they don't change them lightly. So the two stood exchanging harsh words, while the Greeks leaped to their feet with a cry that split the air, divided in opinion about what to do.

"That night we rested and nursed our anger, for Zeus was plotting trouble for us. But in the morning, some of us launched our ships and put our goods and women aboard, while the rest—about half—stayed behind with Agamemnon. We, the other half, embarked and sailed, and the ships went well, for heaven had calmed the sea. When we reached Tenedos we offered sacrifices to the gods, longing to get home. But cruel Zeus didn't yet mean for us to do so, and raised a second quarrel during which some among us turned their ships back and sailed away under Odysseus to make peace with Agamemnon. But I and all the ships with me pressed forward, for I saw that trouble was brewing. Tydeus's son also went on with me, and his crews with him. Later Menelaus joined us at Lesbos and found us deciding our course—for we didn't know whether to go outside Chios by the island of Psyra, keeping it to our left, or inside Chios, past the stormy headland of Mimas. So we asked heaven for a sign and were shown that we'd be soonest out of danger if we headed our ships across the open sea to Euboea. This we did, and a fair wind sprang up that gave us a quick passage during the night to Geraestus, where we offered many sacrifices to Poseidon for helping us so far. Four days later Diomedes and his men stationed their ships in Argos, but I held on for Pylos, and the wind never failed from the day heaven first made it favorable for me.

"Therefore, my dear young friend, I returned without hearing anything about the others. I know neither who got home safely nor who were lost, but as duty requires, I'll give you freely the reports that have reached me since I've been here in my own house. They say the Myrmidons returned home safely under Achilles's son Neoptolemus; so did brave Philoctetes, son of Poias. Idomeneus lost no men at sea, and all his followers who escaped death in battle got safely home with him to Crete. No matter how remote you live, you'll have heard of Agamemnon and the terrible end he met at Aegisthus's hands—and what a fearful reckoning Aegisthus paid for it. See what a good thing it is for a man to leave a son behind him to do as Orestes did, who killed false Aegisthus, his noble father's murderer. You too—for you're a tall, handsome fellow—show your courage and make yourself famous in story."

"Nestor, son of Neleus," Telemachus answered, "honor of the Greek people, the Greeks praise Orestes and his name will live forever, for he nobly avenged his father. Would that heaven might grant me to take similar vengeance on the insolence of the wicked suitors who are mistreating me and plotting my ruin. But the gods have no such happiness in store for my father and me, so we must bear it as best we can."

"My friend," Nestor said, "now that you remind me, I remember hearing that your mother has many suitors who are hostile to you and destroying your estate. Do you submit to this meekly, or are public opinion and heaven's voice against you? Who knows but that Odysseus may return after all and pay these scoundrels in full, either alone or with a force of Greeks behind him? If Athena were to favor you as much as she did Odysseus when we were fighting before Troy—for I never saw the gods so openly fond of anyone as Athena was of your father—if she would take as good care of you as she did of him, some of these suitors would soon forget their courtship."

Telemachus answered, "I can't expect anything like that. It would be far too much to hope for. I don't dare think of it. Even if the gods themselves willed it, no such good fortune could happen to me."

At this Athena said, "Telemachus, what are you talking about? Heaven has a long reach when it wants to save a man. If it were me, I wouldn't care how much I suffered before getting home, as long as I could be safe once I was there. I'd rather that than get home quickly and then be killed in my own house as Agamemnon was by the treachery of Aegisthus and his wife. Still, death is certain, and when a man's time comes, not even the gods can save him, no matter how fond of him they are."

"Mentor," Telemachus answered, "let's not talk about it anymore. There's no chance of my father ever coming back—the gods long ago decided on his destruction. There's something else I'd like to ask Nestor about, since he knows much more than anyone else. They say he's ruled for three generations, so it's like talking to an immortal. Tell me, therefore, Nestor, and tell me truly: how did Agamemnon die that way? What was Menelaus doing? And how did false Aegisthus manage to kill a man so much better than himself? Was Menelaus away from Greek Argos, traveling elsewhere among mankind, so that Aegisthus took courage and killed Agamemnon?"

"I'll tell you truly," Nestor answered, "and you've already guessed how it all happened. If Menelaus had found Aegisthus still alive in his house when he returned from Troy, there would have been no burial mound heaped up for him—not even when he was dead. He would have been thrown outside the city for dogs and vultures, and no woman would have mourned him, for he had committed a terrible crime. But we were over there fighting hard at Troy, and Aegisthus, taking his ease quietly in the heart of Argos, seduced Agamemnon's wife Clytemnestra with constant flattery.

"At first she wanted nothing to do with his wicked scheme, for she was naturally good. Moreover, there was a bard with her whom Agamemnon had strictly ordered, when leaving for Troy, to guard his wife. But when heaven decreed her destruction, Aegisthus took this bard to a desert island and left him there for crows and seagulls to devour—after which she went willingly enough to Aegisthus's house. Then he offered many burnt sacrifices to the gods and decorated many temples with tapestries and gold, for he had succeeded far beyond his expectations.

"Meanwhile Menelaus and I were on our way home from Troy, on good terms with each other. When we reached Sunium, which is the point of Attica, Apollo with his painless arrows killed Phrontis, Menelaus's helmsman—no man knew better how to handle a vessel in rough weather—so he died right there with the helm in his hand. Menelaus, though very anxious to press on, had to wait to bury his comrade and give him proper funeral rites. When he could put to sea again and had sailed as far as the Malean headlands, Zeus plotted evil against him and made it blow hard until the waves ran mountain-high. Here he divided his fleet, taking half toward Crete where the Cydonians live around the waters of the river Iardanus. There's a high headland there stretching into the sea from a place called Gortyn, and all along this coast as far as Phaestus the sea runs high when there's a south wind blowing, but beyond Phaestus the coast is more protected, for a small headland can provide great shelter. Here this part of the fleet was driven onto the rocks and wrecked, but the crews just managed to save themselves. As for the other five ships, they were carried by winds and seas to Egypt, where Menelaus gathered much gold and treasure among people of foreign speech. Meanwhile Aegisthus here at home plotted his evil deed. For seven years after he killed Agamemnon, he ruled in Mycenae with the people obedient to him, but in the eighth year Orestes returned from Athens to be his doom, and killed his father's murderer. Then he held a funeral feast for his mother and false Aegisthus for the people of Argos, and on that very day Menelaus came home with as much treasure as his ships could carry.

"Take my advice then, and don't go traveling far from home for long, leaving your property with such dangerous people in your house. They'll devour everything you have, and you'll have been on a fool's errand. Still, I strongly advise you to go visit Menelaus, who has lately returned from a voyage among such distant peoples that no man could hope to return from, once the winds had carried him so far off course. Even birds can't fly such distances in a year, so vast and terrible are the seas they'd have to cross. Go to him by sea with your own men, or if you'd rather travel by land, you can have a chariot and horses, and here are my sons who can escort you to Lacedaemon where Menelaus lives. Ask him to speak the truth, and he'll tell you no lies, for he's an excellent man."

As he spoke, the sun set and darkness came on, so Athena said, "Sir, all you've said is well. Now, however, order the victims' tongues to be cut and mix wine so we may make drink-offerings to Poseidon and the other immortals, and then go to bed, for it's bedtime. People should leave early and not keep late hours at a religious festival."

Thus spoke Zeus's daughter, and they obeyed her words. Servants poured water over the guests' hands, while pages filled the mixing-bowls with wine and water and handed it around after giving everyone their drink-offering. Then they threw the victims' tongues into the fire and stood up to make their offerings. When they had made their offerings and drunk as much as they wanted, Athena and Telemachus were ready to go aboard their ship, but Nestor immediately stopped them.

"Heaven and the immortal gods forbid," he exclaimed, "that you should leave my house to go aboard a ship! Do you think I'm so poor and short of clothes, or have so few cloaks and blankets that I can't provide comfortable beds for myself and my guests? Let me tell you I have plenty of rugs and cloaks, and won't allow the son of my old friend Odysseus to sleep on a ship's deck—not while I live—nor will my sons after me, but they'll keep open house as I have done."

Then Athena answered, "Sir, you've spoken well, and it will be much better for Telemachus to do as you've said. He'll return with you and sleep at your house, but I must go back to give orders to my crew and keep up their spirits. I'm the only older person among them—the rest are all young men of Telemachus's age who've taken this voyage out of friendship. So I must return to the ship and sleep there. Moreover, tomorrow I must go to the Cauconians, where I have a large sum of money long owed to me. As for Telemachus, since he's now your guest, send him to Lacedaemon in a chariot with one of your sons as escort. Please also provide him with your best and fastest horses."

When she had spoken, she flew away in the form of an eagle, and everyone marveled at the sight. Nestor was astonished and took Telemachus by the hand. "My friend," he said, "I see you're going to be a great hero someday, since the gods attend you while you're still so young. This can have been none other than Zeus's formidable daughter, Athena, who showed such favor to your brave father among the Greeks. Holy queen," he continued, "grant your grace to myself, my good wife, and my children. In return, I'll sacrifice to you a broad-browed heifer, a year old, unbroken and never yet brought under the yoke by man. I'll gild her horns and offer her to you in sacrifice."

Thus he prayed, and Athena heard his prayer. He then led the way to his own house, followed by his sons and sons-in-law. When they'd arrived and taken their places on the benches and seats, he mixed them a bowl of sweet wine that was eleven years old when the housekeeper removed the lid from the jar that held it. As he mixed the wine, he prayed earnestly and made drink-offerings to Athena, daughter of Zeus who bears the aegis. Then, when they'd made their offerings and drunk as much as they wished, the others went home to bed in their own houses. But Nestor put Telemachus to sleep in the room over the gateway along with Pisistratus, who was the only unmarried son he had left. As for himself, he slept in an inner room of the house with the queen his wife beside him.

When rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, Nestor left his bed and took his seat on the benches of white polished marble that stood in front of his house. Here in former times sat Neleus, peer of gods in counsel, but he was now dead and had gone to Hades's house, so Nestor sat in his place with scepter in hand as guardian of the public good. His sons gathered around him as they left their rooms—Echephron, Stratius, Perseus, Aretus, and Thrasymedes. The sixth son was Pisistratus, and when Telemachus joined them, they seated him with them. Nestor then addressed them.

"My sons," he said, "hurry to do as I command you. I want first and foremost to honor the great goddess Athena, who appeared visibly to me during yesterday's festivities. Go, one of you to the plain—tell the herdsman to bring me a heifer and come here with it at once. Another must go to Telemachus's ship and invite all the crew, leaving only two men in charge of the vessel. Someone else will run and fetch Laerces the goldsmith to gild the heifer's horns. The rest of you stay here—tell the maids in the house to prepare an excellent dinner and to bring seats and firewood for a burnt offering. Tell them also to bring me some clear spring water."

At this they hurried off on their various tasks. The heifer was brought from the plain, and Telemachus's crew came from the ship. The goldsmith brought his anvil, hammer, and tongs with which he worked gold, and Athena herself came to accept the sacrifice. Nestor provided the gold, and the smith gilded the heifer's horns so the goddess might take pleasure in their beauty. Then Stratius and Echephron led her in by the horns. Aretus brought water from the house in a decorated pitcher, and in his other hand he held a basket of barley meal. Sturdy Thrasymedes stood by with a sharp ax, ready to strike the heifer, while Perseus held a bowl. Then Nestor began by washing his hands and sprinkling barley meal, offering many prayers to Athena as he threw a lock from the heifer's head into the fire.

When they'd finished praying and sprinkling barley meal, Thrasymedes struck his blow and brought the heifer down with a stroke that cut through the tendons at the base of her neck, at which Nestor's daughters and daughters-in-law, and his venerable wife Eurydice—eldest daughter of Clymenus—cried out with joy. Then they lifted the heifer's head from the ground, and Pisistratus cut her throat. When she'd finished bleeding and was quite dead, they butchered her. They cut out the thigh bones in proper order, wrapped them in two layers of fat, and placed some raw meat on top. Then Nestor laid them on the wood fire and poured wine over them, while the young men stood near him with five-pronged spits in their hands. When the thighs were burned and they'd tasted the inner organs, they cut up the rest of the meat small, put the pieces on spits, and roasted them over the fire.

Meanwhile lovely Polycaste, Nestor's youngest daughter, bathed Telemachus. When she'd washed him and anointed him with oil, she brought him a fine cloak and tunic, and he looked like a god as he came from the bath and took his seat beside Nestor. When the outer meats were done, they drew them off the spits and sat down to dinner, where worthy servants waited on them, pouring wine into golden cups. As soon as they'd eaten and drunk enough, Nestor said, "Sons, harness Telemachus's horses to the chariot so he can start at once."

Thus he spoke, and they did exactly as he said, yoking the swift horses to the chariot. The housekeeper packed them provisions of bread, wine, and delicacies fit for princes. Then Telemachus got into the chariot while Pisistratus gathered up the reins and took the seat beside him. He whipped the horses on, and they flew forward eagerly into the open country, leaving the high citadel of Pylos behind them. All day they traveled, with the yoke swaying on their necks, until the sun set and darkness covered the land. Then they reached Pherae, where Diocles lived—son of Ortilochus and grandson of Alpheus. Here they spent the night, and Diocles entertained them hospitably. When rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, they again harnessed their horses and drove out through the gateway under the echoing portico. Pisistratus whipped the horses on, and they flew forward eagerly. Soon they came to the wheat lands of the open country, and in due time completed their journey, so well did their steeds carry them.

Now when the sun had set and darkness covered the land, Nestor said, "It is getting late; it is time we were all in bed. The libations have been made and the prayers offered; let us go home to rest." Thus he spoke, and they did exactly as he said, yoking the swift horses to the chariot. The housekeeper packed them provisions of bread, wine, and delicacies fit for princes. Then Telemachus got into the chariot while Pisistratus gathered up the reins and took the seat beside him. He whipped the horses on, and they flew forward eagerly into the open country, leaving the high citadel of Pylos behind them. Here they spent the night, and Diocles entertained them hospitably. When rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, they again harnessed their horses and drove out through the gateway under the echoing portico. Pisistratus whipped the horses on, and they flew forward eagerly. Soon they came to the wheat lands of the open country, and in due time completed their journey, so well did their steeds carry them.
